contraindications: Codeine and other opioids in hepatic encephalopathy: avoid.
interactions: Codeine: converted by CYP2D6 to morphine; morphine and its glucuronides accumulate in cirrhosis (reduced hepatic clearance), causing sedation and constipation, both of which precipitate hepatic encephalopathy.
Glipizide: hepatically metabolised; in Child-Pugh C cirrhosis with poor intake it carries a risk of prolonged hypoglycemia, which can mimic or worsen encephalopathy.
Omeprazole: long-term proton pump inhibitor use is associated with hepatic encephalopathy and SBP in cirrhosis; review the indication.
Lactulose and rifaximin: no clinically relevant interaction with spironolactone, furosemide, propranolol, glipizide or omeprazole.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give benzodiazepines or other sedatives for agitation or sleep: they precipitate and prolong hepatic encephalopathy; manage agitation with reorientation, a safe environment and treatment of the precipitant (EASL 2022).
Do not prescribe codeine or other opioids: they precipitate and prolong HE; for pain use acetaminophen up to 2 g per day.
Do not give NSAIDs in cirrhosis with ascites: risk of kidney injury and GI bleeding.
required_recommendations: Identify and treat the precipitants: stop codeine and relieve the constipation with lactulose, adding lactulose enemas and a rectal examination for impaction if there is no bowel movement within 24 hours.

Lactulose 25 mL every 1-2 hours until at least two soft bowel movements, then titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day (ACG 2026 recommendation 10; EASL 2022); avoid over-titration, which causes dehydration, hypokalemia and kidney injury.
Continue rifaximin 550 mg twice daily with lactulose to prevent recurrence (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).
Use acetaminophen up to 2 g per day for pain in place of codeine.

Reserve naloxone for clear opioid toxicity (respiratory depression or pinpoint pupils with depressed consciousness), given in small titrated doses because regular codeine use risks precipitating withdrawal; it is not a diagnostic test for hepatic encephalopathy.
Stop glipizide (risk of prolonged hypoglycemia in Child-Pugh C cirrhosis) and manage the diabetes with insulin and capillary glucose monitoring.
Review omeprazole and stop it unless there is a specific indication: proton pump inhibitors are associated with HE and SBP in cirrhosis (EASL 2022).
Refer for liver transplant assessment: decompensated cirrhosis with recurrent overt HE, MELD-Na 23 (EASL 2018).

Plan HCV treatment with hepatology in relation to transplant listing: in decompensated cirrhosis use sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (with ribavirin where tolerated) and no NS3/4A protease inhibitor (glecaprevir, grazoprevir, voxilaprevir) in Child-Pugh B or C (AASLD-IDSA HCV guidance, 2023 update).
Educate the patient and his wife: no codeine, other opioids or sedatives without medical advice, lactulose adjusted to 2-3 soft stools a day, and early return if confusion recurs.

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade III), hepatitis C cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD-Na 23), precipitated by constipation and codeine accumulation

differential.diagnosis: Opioid (codeine) toxicity as the sole cause
differential.key_features: Codeine is a precipitant, but there is no opioid toxidrome (pupils 3 mm and reactive, respiratory rate 16) and asterixis with triphasic waves indicates a metabolic encephalopathy.
Excluded: ascitic PMN 114 cells/mm3, Gram stain negative, culture no growth.
Plausible on a sulfonylurea in Child-Pugh C cirrhosis, but glucose is 84 mg/dL.
INR 2.0 and platelets 88 raise the risk, but there is no focal deficit or trauma, and CT if obtained shows no blood.
EEG shows diffuse slowing with triphasic waves attenuated by alerting, without epileptiform discharges.
Abstinent for 2 years; serum ethanol not detected.

key_clinical_evidence: Child-Pugh C (13: bilirubin 6.8 3, albumin 2.4 3, INR 2.0 2, small ascites 2, HE grade 3 3); MELD-Na 23 (creatinine 1.0, bilirubin 6.8, INR 2.0, sodium 134)

HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading, evidence of liver dysfunction and exclusion of other causes of altered mental status (ACG 2026; EASL 2022). Somnolence with disorientation to place and time is grade III.

An elevated ammonia neither grades nor confirms hepatic encephalopathy and repeat levels are not used to guide treatment; a normal ammonia in a confused patient with cirrhosis should prompt a search for another cause (ACG 2026 recommendation 5 and key concept 14; EASL 2022).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleeding, electrolyte disturbance, constipation, sedatives and opioids, dehydration and kidney injury (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).
Opioids precipitate HE through central depression and constipation; codeine is converted to morphine, whose clearance falls in cirrhosis, so it accumulates.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A positive opiate screen confirms the codeine exposure, which is a precipitant; it does not mean opioid toxicity explains the encephalopathy. Stop codeine and treat HE with lactulose; naloxone is not a diagnostic test.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute the confusion to opioid toxicity alone and treat with naloxone instead of treating HE and its precipitants.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. C. is a 64-year-old Asian man with hepatitis C cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD-Na 22 at his last hepatology review) awaiting DAA therapy who was brought to the emergency department by his wife for progressive confusion and memory difficulty over 72 hours. The wife reports he has been increasingly confused since three days ago. He has not had a bowel movement in 5 days and has been in abdominal pain from severe constipation. The wife reveals that she gave him extra codeine phosphate 30 mg doses, up to 4 doses per day over the past 3 days, for his abdominal pain from constipation. He is prescribed codeine PRN; the wife was not aware it could be harmful for him. He has had no fever.
